Greedily merging the pairs that raise modularity most stops at the two clusters, drawn as tinted regions in the accent color and teal. The card lists community 0 as A, B, C and community 1 as D, E, F, G." width="100%"} This is a greedy modularity optimization algorithm that merges communities to maximize modularity. It's efficient for medium to large graphs and provides good quality communities. Only works with undirected graphs. Algorithm: 1. start with each node in its own community 2. build a heap of merge candidates ordered by modularity gain (ΔQ) 3. repeatedly merge the pair with highest ΔQ until no improvement 4. return the partition with maximum modularity Edge weights are used on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`). The results match NetworkX's `community.greedy_modularity_communities()` in modularity. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [resolution]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The resolution parameter `γ` of modularity. Merges are scored by `ΔQ = w_ij / m − 2γ a_i a_j`, so values above `1.0` stop merging earlier and give more, smaller communities, while values below `1.0` give fewer, larger ones. Default is `1.0` (standard modularity). [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : column name to store community assignments in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `cmty_fast_greedy`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to community IDs (0-indexed). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If graph is directed (requires undirected graph). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Fast Greedy (Clauset, Newman, and Moore, 2004) maintains a heap of merge candidates ranked by the modularity gain $\Delta Q$ their union would produce, repeatedly pops the top pair, and stops once every candidate merge would strictly decrease modularity. The resulting partition is the one of maximum modularity along that greedy trajectory. This implementation keeps one heap entry per community holding an upper bound on its best gain; since a merge can only lower the gains of pairs it does not touch, stale bounds are re-checked lazily when they reach the top. On sparse graphs the heap bookkeeping runs in $O(n \log^2 n)$ time with $O(n + m)$ memory, which made it the first modularity optimizer usable on graphs of a few hundred thousand nodes. Modern alternatives like Louvain (`cmty_louvain()`) typically reach higher modularity at similar or better cost, but Fast Greedy remains attractive when a strictly agglomerative dendrogram is useful. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two disconnected triangles are the clearest possible case: each becomes its own community, with no edges at all between them: ::: {#fab5715d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # Clique 1 ("D", "E")]) # Clique 2 ) communities = graph.cmty_fast_greedy(return_dict=True) len(set(communities.values())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Raising `resolution=` makes merging stricter. On Zachary's karate club, the default finds three communities, and `resolution=1.5` splits the network further: ::: {#c27340ff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ec.karate_club() ( len(set(karate.cmty_fast_greedy(return_dict=True).values())), len(set(karate.cmty_fast_greedy(resolution=1.5, return_dict=True).values())), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, 5) ``` ::: ::: Storing the result as a node attribute and chaining into `colorize_node_attrs()` visualizes the communities directly: ::: {#f6d2b412 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # Clique 1 ("D", "E")]) # Clique 2 ) ( graph .cmty_fast_greedy(attr_name="community") .colorize_node_attrs(node_attr_from="community", palette="Set1") .describe() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of nodes : 5 Number of edges : 4 Directed : False Density : 0.40 Average degree (min, max) : 1.60 (1, 2) Connected : False Number of connected components : 2 Tree : False Bipartite : False Computations: - cmty_fast_greedy() -> attr: 'community' (5 of 5 nodes) Node aesthetics: - color <- community via colorize (palette: "Set1") (values: #377eb8, #e41a1c, 5 of 5 nodes) ``` ::: :::
